B07C181.summary: Dhritarashtra asks why Karna never used Indra's dart against Krishna or Arjuna when he had the chance. Sanjaya blames fate, saying the plan was made every night and forgotten every morning. After Ghatotkacha's death Yudhishthira is overcome with grief and rushes at Karna, until Vyasa stops him and urges him to keep to virtue and fight on.

scenes.B07C181S01: Dhritarashtra questions Sanjaya about Karna's unused dart, Sanjaya explains the failure, and Vyasa halts Yudhishthira's rush toward Karna.

shots.B07C181S01H01: Dhritarashtra says Karna and Duryodhana acted against sound policy by not using the dart earlier on Krishna or Arjuna.
shots.B07C181S01H02: Sanjaya says the Kaurava warriors resolved each night to use the dart the next morning, but forgot the resolve each day, which he takes as a sign of destiny.
shots.B07C181S01H03: Dhritarashtra blames fate, Krishna and their own folly for the situation, notes the dart is spent on Ghatotkacha, and asks how the battle went on against Drona and the Pandava forces.
shots.B07C181S01H04: Sanjaya describes the Kaurava joy at Ghatotkacha's death and Yudhishthira's grief, which Krishna tries to lift. Yudhishthira answers by recalling Ghatotkacha's services and vows to take revenge on Karna.
shots.B07C181S01H05: Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that Arjuna's survival is a relief, that Ghatotkacha's death served a larger purpose, and that he should stay with virtue and fight the Kauravas. Then Vyasa vanishes.

B07C182.summary: Yudhishthira, still stung by Ghatotkacha's death, orders his whole army to attack Drona, and Duryodhana rushes to protect him. The fighting drags on until both armies are worn out and fall asleep at midnight. Arjuna calls a halt so both sides can rest, and the battle resumes only once the moon rises.

scenes.B07C182S01: Yudhishthira orders a general attack on Drona, both armies tire and sleep, Arjuna calls a truce, and the battle restarts when the moon rises.

shots.B07C182S01H01: Heading: a section title for the Drona-vadha Parva.
shots.B07C182S01H02: Yudhishthira orders his commanders to attack Drona with all their forces, and Duryodhana rushes to guard him. The fighting goes on until both armies are exhausted and many warriors drift into sleep. Arjuna calls for a rest, the Kauravas agree, and both sides stop fighting until the moon rises and the battle picks up again.

B07C183.summary: Duryodhana angrily tells Drona that he has spared the Pandavas and let them grow strong. Drona answers that he will fight to the end, swears to slay the Panchalas, and praises Arjuna's prowess. He then tells Duryodhana to face Arjuna himself and mocks Karna's boasting, and the battle begins again.

scenes.B07C183S01: Duryodhana rebukes Drona for going easy on the Pandavas, Drona praises Arjuna and mocks Karna and the others, and the fighting resumes.

shots.B07C183S01H01: Sanjaya says Duryodhana, in anger, goes to Drona to stir both his wrath and his spirit.
shots.B07C183S01H02: Duryodhana complains that Drona spared the weary Pandavas, who have now grown stronger, and says Drona alone could destroy the three worlds with his weapons.
shots.B07C183S01H03: Drona, angered, answers that he will fight to the limit of his strength and swears to slay the Panchalas, then praises Arjuna's feats in several past battles.
shots.B07C183S01H04: Drona tells Duryodhana to go against Arjuna and mocks Karna, Sakuni, Duhsasana and Duryodhana's boasts. He urges them to fight the Pandavas now, and the battle starts.

B07C184.summary: The battle resumes at dawn, with the Kaurava army split in two. Arjuna, urged on by Krishna and Bhima, forces his way into the Kaurava front, while Drona goes off to the north and wins a series of duels, killing Drupada, Virata and Drupada's three grandsons. Dhrishtadyumna swears to kill Drona or die, and Bhima charges Drona's division as the sun rises.

scenes.B07C184S01: At dawn the armies reform and fight, Arjuna breaks into the Kaurava front, Drona kills several Pandava allies, and Dhrishtadyumna and Bhima take on Drona as the sun comes up.

shots.B07C184S01H01: Sanjaya describes the dawn restart of the battle, the Kaurava army divided into two, and Krishna directing Arjuna to keep Drona's division on his right. Bhima then speaks to Arjuna.
shots.B07C184S01H02: Bhima urges Arjuna to break Drona's division, saying a warrior must now prove his worth and repay his debt to truth and fame.
shots.B07C184S01H03: Arjuna pushes into the Kaurava front while Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni rain arrows on him. Drona moves north and kills Drupada, Virata and Drupada's grandsons, then defeats several other allied kingdoms. Dhrishtadyumna swears an oath to kill Drona or die trying, and Bhima turns on him.
shots.B07C184S01H04: Bhima rebukes Dhrishtadyumna for standing idle, then charges into Drona's army himself. The fight becomes very fierce as the morning sun rises.

B07C185.summary: With the sun up, the fighting restarts among the same warriors who fought in the night. The field turns into a scene of mass slaughter, and dust hides every landmark and every face, so that men strike whoever they touch. The chapter ends with the great warriors facing off in pairs while the surrounding troops watch.

scenes.B07C185S01: After sunrise the battle grows into a vast slaughter under dust, and the main warriors pair off, with Duryodhana fighting Nakula.

shots.B07C185S01H01: Sanjaya says the battle restarts at sunrise and describes the uproar, the piles of weapons and bodies, a river of blood, and the dust that hides the whole field. The great warriors then pair off in fights, and the chapter closes on a scene of the dead, compared with a starry sky.
shots.B07C185S01H02: Duryodhana and Nakula meet in a fight. Nakula shoots at Duryodhana, who turns and drives him back, and Nakula calls out to him to wait, recalling the wrongs Duryodhana has done.

B07C186.summary: Sahadeva kills Duhsasana's driver, leaving Duhsasana to drive on alone, and Bhima and Karna trade blows with maces and arrows until Karna wrecks Bhima's car. Drona and Arjuna then fight an even duel, each matching the other, while gods and seers watch from the sky. The duel ends with both invoking the Brahma weapon, and the general melee resumes.

scenes.B07C186S01: Sahadeva beheads Duhsasana's driver, Karna wrecks Bhima's car after a mace duel, and Drona and Arjuna fight a long duel that ends in a general melee.

shots.B07C186S01H01: Sanjaya tells how Sahadeva cuts off Duhsasana's driver without being noticed, leaving Duhsasana to drive alone. Karna then fights Bhima with arrows and maces, destroying Bhima's car, standard and steeds, so Bhima leaps into Nakula's car.
shots.B07C186S01H02: Drona and Arjuna, teacher and pupil, fight a duel in which each matches the other's weapons. Gods, seers and celestial beings watch and praise them. Drona invokes the Brahma weapon, Arjuna answers with his own, and the duel turns into a general battle that darkens the sky with arrows.

B07C187.summary: Duhsasana is driven back by Dhrishtadyumna while the warriors on both sides keep to fair weapons. Duryodhana and Satyaki, old friends from childhood, meet in a duel and reproach each other for fighting, and Satyaki wounds Duryodhana. Bhima and Karna fight until both cars are wrecked, and Yudhishthira and the twins press the Pandavas to drive the Kauravas away from Drona.

scenes.B07C187S01: Duhsasana is pushed back by Dhrishtadyumna, Duryodhana and Satyaki duel while recalling their friendship, Karna and Bhima fight, and the Pandavas press on to break Drona's guard.

shots.B07C187S01H01: Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna driving Duhsasana back, the warriors on both sides fighting fairly with no unfair weapons, and Duryodhana and Satyaki, boyhood friends, meeting in battle. They reproach each other for fighting, and Duryodhana laments the power of time and the lust for wealth.
shots.B07C187S01H02: Satyaki answers that a warrior must fight even his teachers and invites Duryodhana to kill him. The two duel, Satyaki wounds Duryodhana, and Karna and Bhima fight until both have lost their cars' wheels and weapons. Yudhishthira then urges the Pandava allies on, and Bhima and the twins ask Arjuna to clear the Kurus away from Drona.

B07C188.summary: Drona slaughters great numbers of Panchalas and Srinjayas, and the Pandavas despair of beating him. Krishna proposes a lie: they should tell Drona that his son Aswatthama is dead so he will stop fighting. Bhima kills an elephant named Aswatthama and tells Drona his son is dead, and Yudhishthira is persuaded to confirm it, so Drona is left broken and unable to fight.

scenes.B07C188S01: Drona kills huge numbers of Panchalas, the sages urge him to lay down arms, and he asks Yudhishthira whether his son is dead.

shots.B07C188S01H01: Sanjaya describes Drona's massacre of the Panchalas and Srinjayas, the Pandavas' despair, and Krishna's suggestion that they claim Aswatthama is dead. Bhima kills an elephant of that name and tells Drona his son is dead. Drona doubts the news but, after being stung by it, fights on. Then sages ask him to lay down his arms, and he turns to Yudhishthira to ask whether the news is true.
shots.B07C188S01H02: Krishna urges Yudhishthira to tell a lie to save the army, and Bhima says that Drona will stop fighting if he hears the news from him. Yudhishthira says that Aswatthama is dead, muttering the word elephant. His chariot then touches the ground, and Drona, grief-stricken, can no longer fight Dhrishtadyumna as before.

B07C189.summary: Dhrishtadyumna, the prince born to kill Drona, attacks him with a fierce bow and arrow. Drona, grieving and running short of weapons, holds him off, disarms him again and again, and wounds his horses. Dhrishtadyumna keeps fighting on foot with a sword and shield, until Satyaki intercepts Drona's shaft and saves him, and Arjuna and Krishna praise Satyaki.

scenes.B07C189S01: Dhrishtadyumna and Drona duel back and forth, Drona disarms and wounds him, Dhrishtadyumna keeps fighting with a sword, and Satyaki saves him from Drona's arrow.

shots.B07C189S01H01: Sanjaya describes Dhrishtadyumna's duel with Drona, Drona's dwindling weapons and grief, Dhrishtadyumna's sword work, Satyaki's rescue of the prince, and the praise Arjuna and Krishna give him.

B07C190.summary: Yudhishthira orders his men to attack Drona, who sees bad omens and realizes his end is near. After Bhima rebukes him, Drona lays down his weapons and sits in meditation, and Dhrishtadyumna cuts off his head. The Kuru army scatters and the Pandavas celebrate.

scenes.B07C190S01: Yudhishthira sends his men against Drona, Bhima rebukes Drona, Drona lays down his arms and dies in meditation, and the army breaks up after Dhrishtadyumna kills him.

shots.B07C190S01H01: Sanjaya narrates the whole climax: Satyaki's fight with the Kuru leaders, Yudhishthira's order to attack Drona, the omens, Drona's Brahma weapon, Bhima's rebuke, Drona's death in meditation, and the Kaurava flight and Pandava joy. He says he saw this through Vyasa's grace.

B07C191.summary: After Drona falls, the Kaurava army breaks and flees in panic, with leaders such as Sakuni, Karna, Salya, Kripa and Duryodhana all retreating. Only Aswatthama charges at the Pandava forces. Kripa then tells Aswatthama and Duryodhana how Drona was tricked into laying down his weapons and killed, and Aswatthama bursts into rage.

scenes.B07C191S01: The Kauravas flee in panic after Drona's death, Kripa explains how Drona was deceived and killed, and Aswatthama's anger flares.

shots.B07C191S01H01: Sanjaya describes the Kaurava army falling apart after Drona's death, with the leaders and their divisions fleeing, and soldiers abandoning their armour and chariots while calling on each other to stand.
shots.B07C191S01H02: Aswatthama alone charges the Pandava forces and fights them. Asked by him what has happened, Duryodhana is too ashamed and grief-stricken to speak, so he asks Kripa to explain.
shots.B07C191S01H03: Kripa tells how Drona used the Brahma weapon and how the Pandavas, urged on by Krishna, lied to him that Aswatthama had been slain. He then describes Yudhishthira's half-spoken word, Drona laying down his weapons, and Dhrishtadyumna beheading him despite Arjuna's pleas.
shots.B07C191S01H04: Sanjaya says that on hearing his father's death, Aswatthama burns with fury, grinds his teeth and breathes like an enraged snake, his eyes red as blood.

B07C192.summary: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how Aswatthama reacted to his father's killing by Dhrishtadyumna. He praises Aswatthama's mastery of weapons, comparing him to Drona, Karna and other great warriors. The short chapter ends with the question and sets up Aswatthama's response.

scenes.B07C192S01: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how Aswatthama responded to Drona's death, praising the young man's skill and calling him a second Drona.

shots.B07C192S01H01: Dhritarashtra asks what Aswatthama said on hearing that Drona was killed unrighteously by Dhrishtadyumna, and praises Aswatthama's mastery of weapons and strength in battle.
shots.B07C192S01H02: Heading: marks the start of Section CXCVI.

B07C193.summary: Aswatthama, enraged by his father's death, swears to kill Dhrishtadyumna and wipe out the Panchalas and Pandavas. He recalls that his father received the Narayana weapon from the god, and claims that he alone can now use it. The Kuru army rallies at his words, and he prepares to invoke the weapon.

scenes.B07C193S01: Aswatthama vows vengeance on Dhrishtadyumna and the Pandavas, recounts how he inherited the Narayana weapon, and prepares to use it as the Kuru army rallies.

shots.B07C193S01H01: Aswatthama, blazing with rage, vows to kill Dhrishtadyumna and Yudhishthira, boasts of his prowess, and tells the story of the Narayana weapon that the god gave his father. The Kuru army rallies to his words, and he invokes the weapon after washing with water.

B07C194.summary: The Narayana weapon brings storms, omens and terror to the field, and the Kaurava army rallies behind Aswatthama. Yudhishthira asks Arjuna who is leading the rally, and Arjuna names Aswatthama and bitterly blames Yudhishthira for the lie that led Drona to lay down his arms. Arjuna then says he now regrets the killing so deeply that death seems better than life.

scenes.B07C194S01: The Narayana weapon brings omens, Dhritarashtra asks about the Pandava plan, Yudhishthira questions Arjuna about the rally, and Arjuna names Aswatthama and expresses his remorse over Drona.

shots.B07C194S01H01: Sanjaya describes the omens that come with the Narayana weapon, including storms, rivers running backward, darkness and carrion birds, which frighten gods and men alike.
shots.B07C194S01H02: Dhritarashtra asks what the Pandavas did to protect Dhrishtadyumna once the Kauravas came back to battle under Aswatthama.
shots.B07C194S01H03: Yudhishthira describes the Kaurava rout and asks Arjuna who has rallied the army, since the roaring sound seems like Indra himself has come.
shots.B07C194S01H04: Arjuna names Aswatthama and explains the omen of his birth. He then blames Yudhishthira's half-truth for Drona's fall, says Dhrishtadyumna's act was cruel, and declares that he now feels so guilty that death seems preferable to life.

B07C195.summary: Bhima rebukes Arjuna for speaking of virtue and for praising Aswatthama, insisting that a Kshatriya must defend himself and his brothers. Dhrishtadyumna defends his killing of Drona as deserved and urges Arjuna not to reproach him. Bhima says he will fight Aswatthama alone, and Dhrishtadyumna ends by telling Arjuna to fight now.

scenes.B07C195S01: Bhima rebukes Arjuna for his remorse and vows to fight Aswatthama alone, Dhrishtadyumna defends his killing of Drona, and Arjuna is urged to fight.

shots.B07C195S01H01: Bhima angrily rebukes Arjuna for preaching virtue and praising Aswatthama, reminds him of the Pandavas' wrongs, and boasts that he alone will defeat Aswatthama. Dhrishtadyumna then defends the killing of Drona as just punishment and tells Arjuna not to reproach him, urging him to fight, which he says will bring victory.

B07C196.summary: Dhritarashtra laments that no Kshatriya avenged Drona and asks how the Pandavas reacted. Satyaki furiously accuses Dhrishtadyumna of murdering a Brahmana and of a disgraceful crime, and Dhrishtadyumna replies by listing unfair acts on both sides, including Satyaki's killing of the disarmed Bhurisravas. Satyaki charges with his mace until Bhima restrains him, and Sahadeva, Vasudeva and Yudhishthira calm the two and send them back to battle.

scenes.B07C196S01: Dhritarashtra asks how the Pandavas reacted, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna trade insults, Satyaki charges, and Bhima, Sahadeva and Krishna calm the quarrel.

shots.B07C196S01H01: Dhritarashtra laments that no Kshatriya avenged Drona's death and asks Sanjaya what the Pandavas said to Dhrishtadyumna.
shots.B07C196S01H02: Sanjaya says the assembly stays silent, Arjuna reproaches Dhrishtadyumna with a glance, and Satyaki angrily calls him a sinful murderer of his teacher, threatening him with his mace.
shots.B07C196S01H03: Dhrishtadyumna answers scornfully, saying he forgives Satyaki, then accuses him of killing the disarmed Bhurisravas, and lists the unfair acts of both sides in the war, urging Satyaki to fight.
shots.B07C196S01H04: Satyaki, trembling with rage, charges Dhrishtadyumna with his mace. Bhima seizes him and holds him back, while Sahadeva urges him to forgive and recalls the friendship between their peoples.
shots.B07C196S01H05: Dhrishtadyumna taunts Satyaki and demands to be let go so they can fight. Krishna and Yudhishthira then calm both men, and the Pandava army returns to battle.

B07C197.summary: Aswatthama goes on a rampage, repeats his vow, and invokes the Narayana weapon, which overwhelms the Pandava army. Yudhishthira orders his men to flee and vows to die with his brothers, while Krishna tells everyone to lay down their weapons. Bhima refuses to surrender, insisting he alone will face the weapon, and is struck down by it as Arjuna refuses to use Gandiva against it.

scenes.B07C197S01: Aswatthama unleashes the Narayana weapon, Yudhishthira despairs, Krishna orders the troops to disarm, and Bhima alone takes on the weapon and is overwhelmed.

shots.B07C197S01H01: Sanjaya describes Aswatthama's massacre, his vow to destroy the Pandavas and kill Dhrishtadyumna, the Kaurava rally, and the Narayana weapon's assault on the Pandava army. Yudhishthira then mourns Drona and orders retreat, Krishna tells the troops to lay down their arms, Bhima refuses and charges, Arjuna keeps his bow lowered, and Bhima is overwhelmed by the weapon's fire.

B07C198.summary: Arjuna blunts the Narayana weapon by shielding Bhima and persuading him to dismount and lay down his arms, so the weapon subsides. Aswatthama, who cannot reuse the weapon, fights a long and bloody battle with the Pandava chiefs before Arjuna answers his fire with the Brahma weapon. Aswatthama then flees and asks Vyasa why his weapons failed, and Vyasa explains the divine nature of Krishna and Arjuna.

scenes.B07C198S01: Arjuna and Krishna calm the Narayana weapon by making Bhima lay down his arms, and Aswatthama, unable to use the weapon again, renews the fight and wounds several Pandava warriors.
scenes.B07C198S02: Aswatthama unleashes the Agneya weapon, Arjuna counters with the Brahma weapon, and Aswatthama asks Vyasa why his weapon failed, which leads Vyasa to explain Narayana and Rudra.
scenes.B07C198S03: Aswatthama bows to Vyasa and withdraws his army, and the chapter closes by recalling Drona's death after five days of battle.

shots.B07C198S01H01: Sanjaya says Arjuna shields Bhima from the Narayana weapon, and Krishna persuades him to step down from his chariot and lay down his arms, after which the weapon is stilled.
shots.B07C198S01H02: The sky clears and the Pandavas re-form. Duryodhana urges Aswatthama to use the weapon again, but Aswatthama says it cannot be used twice and that defeat is worse than death.
shots.B07C198S01H03: Dhritarashtra asks what Aswatthama did next, now that the Pandavas were back in battle order.
shots.B07C198S01H04: Aswatthama, fighting on, wounds Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna, kills several Pandava champions, and fights a fierce duel with Bhima. Bhima's driver is knocked unconscious, and Bhima is carried off the field while the Panchalas flee.
shots.B07C198S01H05: Arjuna, roused by the losses of his allies, challenges Aswatthama to show his might and says he will crush his pride.
shots.B07C198S02H01: Dhritarashtra wonders why Arjuna would speak so harshly to Aswatthama, a man of great merit whom Arjuna loves.
shots.B07C198S02H02: Sanjaya explains that Arjuna's grief and anger at the losses and at Yudhishthira's rebuke drove him to insult Aswatthama. Aswatthama then invokes the Agneya weapon, which darkens the sky and burns the Pandava host.
shots.B07C198S02H03: The Kauravas cheer, and Arjuna answers with the Brahma weapon, which clears the darkness and shows that the Pandava forces are not destroyed. Aswatthama, dismayed, drops his bow and runs, and he meets Vyasa and asks why his weapon failed.
shots.B07C198S02H04: Vyasa begins his answer by telling how Narayana performed long austerities and then worshipped Rudra, praising him with a long hymn.
shots.B07C198S02H05: Vyasa continues that Rudra granted Narayana invincible power, that Arjuna is the sage Nara, that Aswatthama is a portion of Rudra, and that Krishna worships Siva.
shots.B07C198S03H01: Aswatthama bows to Vyasa, withdraws the Kuru army for the night, and the Pandavas also pull back. A closing line says Drona had fought for five days and gone to the realm of Brahma.

B07C199.summary: Dhritarashtra asks what his sons and the Pandavas did after Drona fell. Arjuna tells Vyasa about a blazing figure with a lance who rode ahead of him and routed the enemy, and asks who it was. Vyasa identifies it as Siva, recounts his many names and deeds, and urges Arjuna to fight with Krishna as his protector.

scenes.B07C199S01: Dhritarashtra asks what came next, Arjuna describes the radiant figure that fought before him, and Vyasa identifies it as Siva, praises him at length, and sends Arjuna back to battle.

shots.B07C199S01H01: Dhritarashtra asks what his sons and the Pandavas did after Drona was slain by Dhrishtadyumna.
shots.B07C199S01H02: Sanjaya says Arjuna, after the Kuru rout, tells Vyasa that a blazing figure with a lance always ran ahead of his chariot, breaking the enemy so that Arjuna only finished off what it had already broken, and asks who it was.
shots.B07C199S01H03: Vyasa says Arjuna saw Siva, the first cause and lord of the universe, and urges him to take refuge in Siva. He lists many names and epithets of Siva and notes that no one can stand against a warrior with Siva going before him.
shots.B07C199S01H04: Vyasa retells Siva's deeds: his destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, his destruction of the triple city, and the incident of the child in Parvati's lap. He then explains that Siva is all the gods, lists many of his names and their meanings, and says Krishna showed Arjuna this god in a dream. He ends by telling Arjuna to go and fight, since Krishna is his protector.
shots.B07C199S01H05: Closing line: Sanjaya says Vyasa leaves Arjuna and goes back to where he came from.

B07C200.summary: Sanjaya closes the Drona Parva with a benediction, saying that reciting it brings merit and blessings to every class. The rest of the chunk is the translator's footnotes, which explain names and terms, flag corrupt or variant readings in the Bengal and Bombay editions, and give mythological background. The final heading and the Project Gutenberg license text close the file.

scenes.B07C200S01: The end of the Drona Parva, with Sanjaya's closing benediction and the start of the footnotes.
scenes.B07C200S02: Footnotes 3 to 7 explain a fabulous animal, the sense of a verse on grief and duty, and several variant readings.
scenes.B07C200S03: Footnotes 8 to 12 cover a warrior's knowledge of the body, a phrase about walking behind Drona, and some textual differences.
scenes.B07C200S04: Footnotes 13 to 17 discuss a ready instrument, Arjuna as Drona's pupil, a grammatical construction, Ajatasatru, and Ghatotkacha.
scenes.B07C200S05: Footnotes 18 to 22 explain Hayaraja and other names, a corrupted translation, Jarasandha, and the Parijata tree.
scenes.B07C200S06: Footnotes 23 to 27 discuss why the gods do not destroy the host, several corrupt readings, and the wordiness of comparisons.
scenes.B07C200S07: Footnotes 28 to 32 cover the word for heroic, blows, the nishka coin, a variant reading, and the soldiers sworn to conquer or die.
scenes.B07C200S08: Footnotes 33 to 37 deal with variant readings, possibly missing verses, and the meaning of ekacharas.
scenes.B07C200S09: Footnotes 38 to 42 explain the half-moon shape, a cruel attack on a Brahmana, weapons, and some misprints in the Bengal texts.
scenes.B07C200S10: Footnotes 43 to 47 note corrupt verses, a repeated verse, the sense of not abandoning comrades, and the custom of naming oneself before a fight.
scenes.B07C200S11: Footnotes 48 to 52 cover the spelling of Draupadeyas, several verse differences, and a note on Suparva and Bhagadatta.
scenes.B07C200S12: Footnotes 53 to 57 discuss a corrupted word, free renderings, a Bengal reading of a line, and the meaning of the summer and rainy months.
scenes.B07C200S13: Footnotes 58 to 62 weigh textual readings, the rivalry between Nila and Aswatthaman, and the meaning of dhumaketu.
scenes.B07C200S14: Footnotes 63 to 67 explain car parts, several kinds of arrows, and the names of drums.
scenes.B07C200S15: Footnotes 68 to 72 cover a reading of verse 4, Duhsasana's fate according to Abhimanyu, an elephant in low ground, and car parts.
scenes.B07C200S16: Footnotes 73 to 77 address a slightly different reading, the Kubera simile, an unclear phrase, and the verse numbering.
scenes.B07C200S17: Footnotes 78 to 82 repeat a note on expanding a verse and correct several readings, including tree-tops.
scenes.B07C200S18: Footnotes 83 to 87 explain ritual impurity during mourning, several verse readings, and who speaks the last verses.
scenes.B07C200S19: Footnotes 88 to 92 cover Nilakantha's rendering, the sense of Samvarta, the word for robbers, and rivers of gold.
scenes.B07C200S20: Footnotes 93 to 97 explain sacrifices for Kshatriyas, the Siksha branch of the Vedas, the Kshatriya term, and libations.
scenes.B07C200S21: Footnotes 98 to 102 explain Rama's four kinds of creatures, the sacred ghats, the story of Sagara and Bhagiratha, and a corrected reading.
scenes.B07C200S22: Footnotes 103 to 107 give literal senses, a Bombay variant, the names of sweets, and the methods of Vedic study.
scenes.B07C200S23: Footnotes 108 to 112 explain a fee, animals slain in sacrifice, the Chumbal river, and a begging vessel.
scenes.B07C200S24: Footnotes 113 to 117 explain a golden city, the measure of a vyama, the meaning of Kshatriya and raja, and Siva's bow.
scenes.B07C200S25: Footnotes 118 to 122 explain several terms and point out errors in Bengali translations.
scenes.B07C200S26: Footnotes 123 to 127 explain mail-clad warriors, a reading of a line, twilight as a goddess, and the function of slaps in verse.
scenes.B07C200S27: Footnotes 128 to 132 discuss a reading of verse 9, Karna's support for Jayadratha, a kind of car, and a musical note.
scenes.B07C200S28: Footnotes 133 to 137 cover a misspelled word, the sense of apavritta, and wordy phrasing in the original.
scenes.B07C200S29: Footnotes 138 to 142 note that Sanjaya sometimes fought, explain mantra-based weapons, and comment on Arjuna's speed.
scenes.B07C200S30: Footnotes 143 to 147 include a joke that translators missed, the sense of avabhritha and praviddham, and the three cities of Tripura.
scenes.B07C200S31: Footnotes 148 to 152 correct the reading of arka, explain golden-car owners and nidas, and compare this section with the Bhishma Parva.
scenes.B07C200S32: Footnotes 153 to 157 explain the use of cars as weapons, the twofold fear in the Kuru ranks, a reading of Calada, and the chances of a fight.
scenes.B07C200S33: Footnotes 158 to 162 cover a literal gloss, a better reading, corrected names, the simile of fire and wind, and a probable missing line.
scenes.B07C200S34: Footnotes 163 to 167 explain the phrase for rage, the mountain of herbs and Hanuman, a cow's hoof, and a promise of victory.
scenes.B07C200S35: Footnotes 168 to 172 explain Satyaki's title, an incomplete verse, a literal phrase, and yoga-based death by fasting.
scenes.B07C200S36: Footnotes 173 to 177 explain chakram, the kavandha, a note on the scale, and differences in verse numbering.
scenes.B07C200S37: Footnotes 178 to 182 discuss the Supreme Deity, a triplet, a literal phrase, and Duryodhana's remark about Sikhandin.
scenes.B07C200S38: Footnotes 183 to 187 cover readings, Duryodhana's words to Drona about the Somakas, and a triplet.
scenes.B07C200S39: Footnotes 188 to 192 explain free renderings, a simile of rays and a lake, omitted lines, and drum types.
scenes.B07C200S40: Footnotes 193 to 197 correct readings, identify the brother of the Kalinga prince, explain patanipam, and measure a nalwa.
scenes.B07C200S41: Footnotes 198 to 202 explain Pisachas, Ghatotkacha's family tie to Ashwatthaman, the thunder weapon, Rakshasa kinds, and Tripura.
scenes.B07C200S42: Footnotes 203 to 207 explain asani, correct readings of a verse, Achyuta as a name of Krishna, and triplets.
scenes.B07C200S43: Footnotes 208 to 212 note triplets, correct two readings in verse 4, and prefer Rathanaga over Naranaga.
scenes.B07C200S44: Footnotes 213 to 217 note triplets, a changed reading of a verse, and the translator's choice of faithfulness over elegance.
scenes.B07C200S45: Footnotes 218 to 222 correct readings, explain lokanamabhave and nalikas, and interpret Karna's name as Vaikartana.
scenes.B07C200S46: Footnotes 223 to 227 offer readings, the sense of yena and tena, and a correction of a verse's first line.
scenes.B07C200S47: Footnotes 228 to 232 explain verse numbering, a triplet, the sense of a head as tribute, an arani, and asaktam.
scenes.B07C200S48: Footnotes 233 to 237 explain Rakshasa strength at certain hours, Mainaka, a new lease of life, and the word Jara.
scenes.B07C200S49: Footnotes 238 to 241 discuss Sagadaya, the mouthless gods, and triplets, before the heading that starts Section CXCVI.
scenes.B07C200S50: Footnotes 242 to 246 explain the nine-hour night, a thousand yamas, the moon and the lotus, the east, and Vrishodara.
scenes.B07C200S51: Footnotes 247 to 251 correct a vocative, explain Drona's oath, mark a triplet, and discuss crooked arrows.
scenes.B07C200S52: Footnotes 252 to 256 cover an omitted verse, living celestial weapons, the loss of both worlds, and the Brahma weapon.
scenes.B07C200S53: Footnotes 257 to 261 explain dharmadhwajin, a corrected reading in the Venisamhara lines, and the Bali episode in Rama's story.
scenes.B07C200S54: Footnotes 262 to 266 cover an expanded sense, Vishnu and Hiranyakasipu, the Nishadas, Satyaki's teacher, and kimpurushas.
scenes.B07C200S55: Footnotes 267 to 271 comment on Bombay readings, Siva's epithets, and the phrase source of immortality.
scenes.B07C200S56: Footnotes 272 to 274 explain the five qualities, the bow given to Rama, and the names for Death, before the license text begins.

shots.B07C200S01H01: Sanjaya's closing benediction says that reciting this Parva brings the fruit of Vedic study, freedom from sin, and blessings for each of the social classes.
shots.B07C200S01H02: Heading: marks the end of the Drona Parva.
shots.B07C200S01H04: Footnote 1 gives a literal rendering of a phrase describing the speech as an oration full of unrefined expressions.
shots.B07C200S01H05: Footnote 2 explains that the woman is stripped of robes and ornaments because she is a widow.
shots.B07C200S02H01: Footnote 3 says a Sarabha is a fabulous eight-legged animal supposed to be stronger than the lion.
shots.B07C200S02H02: Footnote 4 reads the verse as meaning that since such a hero is slain, nothing on earth is lasting, so grief over wealth and children is misplaced.
shots.B07C200S02H03: Footnote 5 notes a slight variant in the Bombay text and gives the sense: since all things die, there is no reason to fear doing one's duty.
shots.B07C200S02H04: Footnote 6 notes that the last line is misread in the Bombay text.
shots.B07C200S02H05: Footnote 7 says a word in one verse is misread in the Bengal text, and the Bombay edition gives a different word.
shots.B07C200S03H01: Footnote 8 explains kula-samhanana-jnana as knowledge of the body and its vital parts, which every trained warrior needed.
shots.B07C200S03H02: Footnote 9 glosses a phrase as asking who would feel it humiliating to walk behind Drona.
shots.B07C200S03H03: Footnote 10 notes a major difference between the Bengal and Bombay texts and argues that Karna must have been at the head of the rearguard, just behind Drona.
shots.B07C200S03H04: Footnote 11 explains that the birds wheeled to the left of the Kuru army, which is an evil omen.
shots.B07C200S03H05: Footnote 12 notes the Bengal text adds words, 'nothing could be seen save Drona's arrows', to make the sense clear.
shots.B07C200S04H01: Footnote 13 suggests that a word means a ready instrument.
shots.B07C200S04H02: Footnote 14 gives the sense that Drona, having trained Arjuna, received defeat and death at the hands of, or through, his own pupil.
shots.B07C200S04H03: Footnote 15 explains an unusual grammatical construction in which a pronoun stands in apposition to a noun in the objective case, and says the order of the original is kept.
shots.B07C200S04H04: Footnote 16 notes that verses 10 and 11 also refer to Ajatasatru, that is, Yudhishthira.
shots.B07C200S04H05: Footnote 17 identifies Ghatotkacha as Bhima's son and notes that Rakshasi women give birth on the day they conceive, and their children grow up the day they are born.
shots.B07C200S05H01: Footnote 18 explains Hayaraja as 'prince of steeds', an Asura also called Kesi who took the form of a horse.
shots.B07C200S05H02: Footnote 19 explains a phrase as meaning 'without weapons of any kind'.
shots.B07C200S05H03: Footnote 20 remarks that the Bengali translator Kaliprasanna Singha garbles this verse.
shots.B07C200S05H04: Footnote 21 identifies Jarasandha, king of the Magadhas and enemy of Krishna, as killed by Bhima at Krishna's urging.
shots.B07C200S05H05: Footnote 22 identifies the event as the transplanting of the Parijata tree from Amaravati to the earth.
shots.B07C200S06H01: Footnote 23 explains that the gods, though divine, took human birth and must act by human means, which is why they do not destroy the host by will alone.
shots.B07C200S06H02: Footnote 24 says the Bengal texts misread two words here, and gives the correct readings satatam and asukarinas.
shots.B07C200S06H03: Footnote 25 notes a Bengal and Bombay variant in a compound and explains that vajinas means fowl or bird.
shots.B07C200S06H04: Footnote 26 remarks that the comparisons are pursued so minutely that they weaken their effect, and that the repetitions suit verses composed on the spot.
shots.B07C200S06H05: Footnote 27 says the Bengal text misreads a verse, and that 'hayan' should be 'Dhanus'.
shots.B07C200S07H01: Footnote 28 points out that the word 'heroic' appears in the next verse.
shots.B07C200S07H02: Footnote 29 gives the Sanskrit words for three kinds of blow: sampata, abhighata and nipata.
shots.B07C200S07H03: Footnote 30 explains nishka as a golden coin whose weight varies among authorities.
shots.B07C200S07H04: Footnote 31 chooses the Bengal reading 'Vidhayaivam' over the Bombay reading 'Vihayainam', which would mean 'leaving Yudhishthira'.
shots.B07C200S07H05: Footnote 32 explains the term as soldiers sworn to conquer or die, and suggests repeating the phrase rather than paraphrasing it each time.
shots.B07C200S08H01: Footnote 33 notes that the second line reads differently in the Bombay text.
shots.B07C200S08H02: Footnote 34 suggests the text here is corrupt and that a whole verse seems to be missing.
shots.B07C200S08H03: Footnote 35 says the second line of this verse is corrupt.
shots.B07C200S08H04: Footnote 36 explains ekacharas as those that walk alone and cannot bear their own kind, and notes that some translators take it to mean the rhinoceros.
shots.B07C200S08H05: Footnote 37 gives the literal sense: he thought in his mind that his hour had come.
shots.B07C200S09H01: Footnote 38 explains a term literally as 'half-moon-shaped'.
shots.B07C200S09H02: Footnote 39 says the attack was cruel because Satanika was fighting a Brahmana.
shots.B07C200S09H03: Footnote 40 says the Bengal reading 'Vahupellava' is a mistake and the correct reading is 'Vahupannaga'.
shots.B07C200S09H04: Footnote 41 notes that even such ordinary objects were used as weapons, given Bhima's superhuman might.
shots.B07C200S09H05: Footnote 42 says 'Hemadandais' in the Bengal texts is a mistake for 'Hemabhandiers'.
shots.B07C200S10H01: Footnote 43 says the first line of verse 20 is corrupt in the Bengal texts and the Bombay reading is correct.
shots.B07C200S10H02: Footnote 44 says this seems to repeat the sixth verse.
shots.B07C200S10H03: Footnote 45 explains the phrase as meaning not to abandon comrades in distress.
shots.B07C200S10H04: Footnote 46 says the last word of the first line of a verse is corrupt in the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S10H05: Footnote 47 explains the custom that a warrior gave his name and lineage before striking an opponent.
shots.B07C200S11H01: Footnote 48 notes that the printed texts read 'Drupadeyas' but it should be 'Draupadeyas'.
shots.B07C200S11H02: Footnote 49 says the first line of verse 54 is misread in the Bengal texts, and the Bombay reading is followed.
shots.B07C200S11H03: Footnote 50 says a complete verse in the Bombay text after verse 19 does not appear to be genuine.
shots.B07C200S11H04: Footnote 51 says the second line of verse 46 is omitted in the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S11H05: Footnote 52 says the Bengali translators garble two verses, and the correct reading is 'Suparva' meaning 'of beautiful limbs'; Parvatapati is Bhagadatta.
shots.B07C200S12H01: Footnote 53 says the Bengal reading 'abhitas' is incorrect and should be 'Kshubitas'.
shots.B07C200S12H02: Footnote 54 says verses 16 and 17 are rendered rather freely so that the sense is clear.
shots.B07C200S12H03: Footnote 55 gives the Bengal reading, which would say the warrior is either the first or second on the earth.
shots.B07C200S12H04: Footnote 56 says the Bombay reading 'paritas' is faulty, and the Bengal texts read 'twaritas'.
shots.B07C200S12H05: Footnote 57 discusses a Bengal reading in the second line and explains that 'varsha' means season, so the two months are summer months.
shots.B07C200S13H01: Footnote 58 says the Bengal reading 'Samprapte' is faulty and the Bombay reading 'Sambhrante' is correct.
shots.B07C200S13H02: Footnote 59 says verse 5 is rendered a little freely and expanded to make the sense clear.
shots.B07C200S13H03: Footnote 60 prefers the Bengal reading 'Purvabhilashi' and notes that Nila and Aswatthaman had a rivalry for some time.
shots.B07C200S13H04: Footnote 61 explains that dhumaketu, which the translator had rendered as comet elsewhere, here means fire, since it has smoke for its mark.
shots.B07C200S13H05: Footnote 62 notes that the first half of verse 21 grammatically connects with verse 20.
shots.B07C200S14H01: Footnote 63 says the second half of a line is corrupt in the Bengal texts and gives the correct reading 'ayuduha-viarada'.
shots.B07C200S14H02: Footnote 64 explains janghas as limbs of cars used in battle.
shots.B07C200S14H03: Footnote 65 says the second half of the second line of verse 2 is corrupt in the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S14H04: Footnote 66 lists and explains several kinds of arrows, including razor-sharp, calf-tooth-headed, stout-bodied, long, half-moon-headed and broad-headed.
shots.B07C200S14H05: Footnote 67 explains that these are names of various drums, large and small.
shots.B07C200S15H01: Footnote 68 gives the Bombay reading of the first line of verse 4.
shots.B07C200S15H02: Footnote 69 explains that the 'fruit' is the coming encounter with Abhimanyu, in which Duhsasana is to lose his life, according to Abhimanyu.
shots.B07C200S15H03: Footnote 70 explains pravanddiva as an elephant in low land covered with mud and water.
shots.B07C200S15H04: Footnote 71 notes that these words appear again lower down, in verse 17.
shots.B07C200S15H05: Footnote 72 explains these are parts of cars.
shots.B07C200S16H01: Footnote 73 notes that the Bombay reading is slightly different.
shots.B07C200S16H02: Footnote 74 renders a phrase literally as 'like another son of the Lord of Treasure', meaning Kubera.
shots.B07C200S16H03: Footnote 75 admits the note does not understand the phrase 'asiva vachvz Srijatam' and offers a tentative rendering.
shots.B07C200S16H04: Footnote 76 explains the numbering follows the Bengal texts, and verse 23 consists of three lines.
shots.B07C200S16H05: Footnote 77 says the fifth verse is expanded a little to make the sense clear.
shots.B07C200S17H01: Footnote 78 repeats the note that the fifth verse is expanded a little for clarity.
shots.B07C200S17H02: Footnote 79 says the Bengal text reads the first line of a verse vicious and meaningless, and gives the correct reading.
shots.B07C200S17H03: Footnote 80 says the Bengal text reads 'Taru-tringani', meaning tree-tops.
shots.B07C200S17H04: Footnote 81 gives the correct reading as 'Mahavalan Mahavalat'.
shots.B07C200S17H05: Footnote 82 accepts the Bombay reading 'Valabudhischa' over the Bengal 'Avalabudhischa'.
shots.B07C200S18H01: Footnote 83 explains that during mourning a person is ritually unclean and cannot perform worship until the obsequies are done and he is cleansed.
shots.B07C200S18H02: Footnote 84 notes that the first line of verse 6 is read differently in the Bombay edition, and the Bengal reading is preferred.
shots.B07C200S18H03: Footnote 85 says both editions read 'prita', gratified, but the correct word is 'Bhita', affrighted, which some Bengali translators also adopt.
shots.B07C200S18H04: Footnote 86 explains that 'Devas' in verse 46 means the senses, and 'Vrittas' means men of virtue.
shots.B07C200S18H05: Footnote 87 says verse 55 is incomplete and needs correcting, and argues that verses 55 to 58 are the words of Vyasa, not Sanjaya.
shots.B07C200S19H01: Footnote 88 says the translator follows Nilakantha in rendering two verses.
shots.B07C200S19H02: Footnote 89 gives a literal gloss of a term as 'of golden excreta'.
shots.B07C200S19H03: Footnote 90 prefers the Bengal reading 'Samvartam' and notes that the Bombay text would make Samvarta the subject, and mocks K. P. Singha's blunder.
shots.B07C200S19H04: Footnote 91 explains 'Atavika' as one who dwells in the woods, though it commonly means a thief or robber.
shots.B07C200S19H05: Footnote 92 explains 'Vahinyas' as rivers and 'Swairinyas' as open to all, and notes a reading that would mean rivers of liquid gold.
shots.B07C200S20H01: Footnote 93 explains the term as the sacrifices ordained for Kshatriyas.
shots.B07C200S20H02: Footnote 94 explains Siksha as the Vedic branch of phonetics and akshara as letters, so these Brahmanas were good readers of the Veda.
shots.B07C200S20H03: Footnote 95 explains murddhabhishikta literally as one whose coronal locks have had the investiture rite, and so means a Kshatriya or royal person.
shots.B07C200S20H04: Footnote 96 gives an alternative reading that would mean he poured libations to Indra as copious as water.
shots.B07C200S20H05: Footnote 97 explains that juniors died before their seniors, and notes that the causative form is a license.
shots.B07C200S21H01: Footnote 98 lists the four kinds of creatures that owned Rama's rule: egg-born, womb-born, born of filth, and plants.
shots.B07C200S21H02: Footnote 99 explains that these were ghats, landings that gave access to the sacred stream.
shots.B07C200S21H03: Footnote 100 reads 'Janaughena' for a corrupt word and recounts the story of Sagara's sons, and how Bhagiratha brought the Ganga to save them.
shots.B07C200S21H04: Footnote 101 says the correct reading is 'Valguvadinas', not a genitive plural form.
shots.B07C200S21H05: Footnote 102 notes that the Bombay edition has some extra verses after the third.
shots.B07C200S22H01: Footnote 103 gives the literal sense 'having me for his sustainer'.
shots.B07C200S22H02: Footnote 104 notes that the Bombay text gives 'Puru' in place of 'Suna'.
shots.B07C200S22H03: Footnote 105 notes that the Bengal text reads this verse differently.
shots.B07C200S22H04: Footnote 106 explains that the words in italics name sweets made of wheat or barley, milk, and sugar or honey.
shots.B07C200S22H05: Footnote 107 explains that these are the methods by which he sought to know the Vedas.
shots.B07C200S23H01: Footnote 108 explains 'nakshatra-dakshina' as a fee ordained for the lunar asterism, following Nilakantha.
shots.B07C200S23H02: Footnote 109 says the second line of the second verse is corrupt in the Bengal texts, and the Bombay reading is better.
shots.B07C200S23H03: Footnote 110 explains that animals slain in sacrifice are believed to go to heaven.
shots.B07C200S23H04: Footnote 111 identifies the river with the modern Chumbal.
shots.B07C200S23H05: Footnote 112 explains that a vessel is used by Brahmanas and others for begging.
shots.B07C200S24H01: Footnote 113 explains that 'vaswoksara' means made of gold, and suggests the city of Rantideva is golden.
shots.B07C200S24H02: Footnote 114 explains a vyama as the span between two arms fully stretched.
shots.B07C200S24H03: Footnote 115 explains that a Kshatriya is one who rescues others from wounds and injuries.
shots.B07C200S24H04: Footnote 116 explains that a raja is one who has his people's affection and delights them.
shots.B07C200S24H05: Footnote 117 identifies this as Siva's bow, also called Pinaka.
shots.B07C200S25H01: Footnote 118 explains 'aklishtakarman' as one who never tires of work, able to obtain results by will alone, or one whose acts are unspotted.
shots.B07C200S25H02: Footnote 119 explains 'parthivas' as relating to the earth.
shots.B07C200S25H03: Footnote 120 explains the first line of the verse as Nilakantha paraphrases it.
shots.B07C200S25H04: Footnote 121 notes that the Bombay text adds verses that are not in the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S25H05: Footnote 122 says K. P. Singha makes a ludicrous blunder in reading this line.
shots.B07C200S26H01: Footnote 123 explains 'sannahikas' as warriors clad in mail.
shots.B07C200S26H02: Footnote 124 says the Bengal reading 'Dwijaidhitam' is better than the Bombay 'Dwijochitam'.
shots.B07C200S26H03: Footnote 125 explains that twilight is herself a goddess adored with certain prayers at that time.
shots.B07C200S26H04: Footnote 126 explains that these slaps mark the cadences.
shots.B07C200S26H05: Footnote 127 explains the phrase literally as 'in crossing'.
shots.B07C200S27H01: Footnote 128 rejects the Bengal reading 'Satyavrataiv' in verse 9 as absurd and adopts the Bombay 'Satyaratas'.
shots.B07C200S27H02: Footnote 129 explains that Karna added his voice to Jayadratha's request that Drona protect him.
shots.B07C200S27H03: Footnote 130 explains a term as a kind of car or vehicle.
shots.B07C200S27H04: Footnote 131 suggests that 'tasmai' refers to the Three-eyed god Siva, not to Krishna.
shots.B07C200S27H05: Footnote 132 explains that a term is the second note of the Hindu musical scale.
shots.B07C200S28H01: Footnote 133 says 'Vasavamiva' is a mistake for 'Vasavasyeva'.
shots.B07C200S28H02: Footnote 134 explains 'apavrittam' as endangered or doubtful, and reads the passage as bitter prospects for Duryodhana if his kingdom is taken or handed over after his sons are slain.
shots.B07C200S28H03: Footnote 135 notes that the original is pleonastic, meaning wordy.
shots.B07C200S28H04: Footnote 136 suggests that 'golden coats of mail' needs correcting to coats of black iron decked with gold and dyed with blood.
shots.B07C200S28H05: Footnote 137 notes that the original is pleonastic, meaning wordy.
shots.B07C200S29H01: Footnote 138 notes this verse is in every text, suggesting that Sanjaya sometimes also took part in the fighting.
shots.B07C200S29H02: Footnote 139 says the words 'tatsainyanyabhyapujayan' are meaningless here, and the Bengali translators left them out.
shots.B07C200S29H03: Footnote 140 explains that celestial weapons were forces that depended on mantras, and that ordinary arrows became celestial when charged with them.
shots.B07C200S29H04: Footnote 141 explains that Arjuna's chariot moved through the enemy as fast as his arrows.
shots.B07C200S29H05: Footnote 142 says the first line is vicious in the Bengal texts, and the Bombay reading gives a word meaning the froth in the steeds' mouths.
shots.B07C200S30H01: Footnote 143 explains the phrase as referring to his funeral rites, a joke that the vernacular translators missed.
shots.B07C200S30H02: Footnote 144 gives the sense of this verse without a close literal translation.
shots.B07C200S30H03: Footnote 145 explains that avabhritha is the final bath after a sacrifice, and that Krishna sees Duryodhana's death as the avabhritha of the battle sacrifice.
shots.B07C200S30H04: Footnote 146 explains 'praviddham' as fallen or loosened from its place, following Nilakantha.
shots.B07C200S30H05: Footnote 147 explains that Tripura is the three cities built by the Asura artificer Maya, and that Siva destroyed them with their people.
shots.B07C200S31H01: Footnote 148 says the true reading is 'alohita', not 'lohita', and that 'arka' here means crystal, not the sun.
shots.B07C200S31H02: Footnote 149 glosses a term as owners of golden cars.
shots.B07C200S31H03: Footnote 150 explains 'nidas' as niches or drivers' boxes on a car.
shots.B07C200S31H04: Footnote 151 notes that many opening verses of this section nearly match section 76 of the Bhishma Parva, and that some readings follow the Bombay edition.
shots.B07C200S32H01: Footnote 153 explains the phrase as using cars and elephants as weapons against cars and elephants.
shots.B07C200S32H02: Footnote 154 explains that the fear behind the Kurus came from the Pandava army, and the fear in front came from car-warriors who had broken into the Kuru host.
shots.B07C200S32H03: Footnote 155 notes that many Bengal texts read 'Calabhairiva', a mistake for 'Calada'.
shots.B07C200S32H04: Footnote 156 renders the second line of verse 4 freely, the sense being that no one can say beforehand who will win a fight.
shots.B07C200S32H05: Footnote 157 explains that the first line of verse 14 is given separately, because the two languages have different grammar.
shots.B07C200S33H01: Footnote 158 gives the literal sense 'disregard of Krishna'.
shots.B07C200S33H02: Footnote 159 says the Bombay reading is better than the Bengal one.
shots.B07C200S33H03: Footnote 160 says the Bombay forms are incorrect and reads 'Vrikodaras' and 'navavhis' from the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S33H04: Footnote 161 explains the sense: Karna and Bhima were like fire and wind.
shots.B07C200S33H05: Footnote 162 notes that verse 28 is a triplet, and its second line is obscure, probably because a line is missing.
shots.B07C200S34H01: Footnote 163 gives the literal sense 'mustered all his rage'.
shots.B07C200S34H02: Footnote 164 says the Bengal reading 'Ayastam' is better than the Bombay 'Ayastas' in the first line of verse 62.
shots.B07C200S34H03: Footnote 165 explains that the mountain overgrown with healing herbs alludes to Hanuman's removal of Gandhamadana to cure Lakshmana.
shots.B07C200S34H04: Footnote 166 explains a phrase as the small indent made by a cow's hoof.
shots.B07C200S34H05: Footnote 167 explains that whoever slays the speaker will always win battles and never be defeated.
shots.B07C200S35H01: Footnote 168 explains that Satyaki is called 'of true prowess', and if he is defeated by Bhurisravas that title would be falsified.
shots.B07C200S35H02: Footnote 169 says verse 20 is incomplete and the translator supplies a phrase, and notes that the first line of verse 21 connects with verse 20.
shots.B07C200S35H03: Footnote 170 gives the literal sense: who could watch Satyaki reduced to that plight with indifference?
shots.B07C200S35H04: Footnote 171 explains that dying by abstaining from food is a yogic way of freeing the soul from the body.
shots.B07C200S35H05: Footnote 172 gives the literal sense: near the place assigned for the sacrificial butter.
shots.B07C200S36H01: Footnote 173 explains 'chakram' as 'prowess' in Nilakantha's gloss.
shots.B07C200S36H02: Footnote 174 says the second line of verse 94 is rendered a little freely to make the sense clearer.
shots.B07C200S36H03: Footnote 175 explains a kavandha as a headless trunk that moves as if alive, and notes tales of such beings drinking the blood of victims.
shots.B07C200S36H04: Footnote 176 explains that this is the second of the seven notes of the Hindu scale.
shots.B07C200S36H05: Footnote 177 notes that editions disagree on the order and numbering of the last dozen verses, and that Bombay omits a few.
shots.B07C200S37H01: Footnote 178 explains that everything, even inanimate creation, exists and worships the Supreme Deity.
shots.B07C200S37H02: Footnote 179 notes that this is a triplet in the Calcutta edition.
shots.B07C200S37H03: Footnote 180 gives the literal sense: 'the fact of the Dhartarashtras having sunk into distress'.
shots.B07C200S37H04: Footnote 181 gives the literal sense: 'of persons whose coronal locks have undergone the sacred bath'.
shots.B07C200S37H05: Footnote 182 explains that Nilakantha reads a word as Duryodhana calling Sikhandin a deceitful hunter for the trick used against Bhishma, which the note finds far-fetched.
shots.B07C200S38H01: Footnote 183 says the translator adopts the Bombay reading.

shots.B07C200S42H03: Footnote 205 explains that 'Achyuta', used as a name, refers to Krishna, meaning 'of unfading glory' or 'the immortal'.

shots.B07C200S43H04: Footnote 211 says the Bengal reading 'sudakshinas' does not seem right, and the Bombay reading 'sudarnnam' is adopted.
shots.B07C200S43H05: Footnote 212 notes that the Bombay and Bengal texts differ in the first line of verse 3, and that 'Rathanaga' is the correct reading, not 'Naranaga'.

shots.B07C200S44H05: Footnote 217 remarks that the Bombay readings are generally better, that many verses have wordy and faulty syntax, and that the translator chose faithfulness over elegance.

shots.B07C200S46H05: Footnote 227 says that 'Vaganais' rather than 'Vanaganan' is the true reading in the first line of verse 30.

shots.B07C200S47H02: Footnote 229 notes that this is a triplet in the Bengal texts.

shots.B07C200S48H01: Footnote 233 notes that the second line of verse 85 is read differently in the Bombay edition.

shots.B07C200S48H04: Footnote 236 explains that they believed they had received a new lease of life.
shots.B07C200S48H05: Footnote 237 explains that the word literally means 'united by Jara'.

shots.B07C200S49H02: Footnote 239 explains that because fire is the mouth of the gods, without fire the gods would be mouthless, following Nilakantha.

shots.B07C200S50H02: Footnote 243 gives the literal sense of 'of a thousand Yamas'.
shots.B07C200S50H03: Footnote 244 explains that the moon is lord of lilies because lilies bloom at moonrise, as the sun is lord of lotuses, and that the direction presided over by Indra is the east.
shots.B07C200S50H04: Footnote 245 explains that 'dasatakasha-kkupa' means the quarter presided over by Indra, the east.
shots.B07C200S50H05: Footnote 246 notes that the Bombay text reads 'Vrishottama' instead of 'Vrishodara', and the translator adopts it.
shots.B07C200S51H01: Footnote 247 says the Bengal form 'Rajanam' should be 'Rujendra', the vocative form found in the Bombay edition.
shots.B07C200S51H02: Footnote 248 says the translator renders this too freely; the oath means that whoever Drona lets escape alive, or whoever he defeats, should be ruined.
shots.B07C200S51H03: Footnote 249 notes that this is a triplet in the Bengal texts.
shots.B07C200S51H04: Footnote 250 says the translator adopts the Bombay reading of the first line of this verse.
shots.B07C200S51H05: Footnote 251 explains that arrows of crooked course were condemned because they could not be baffled easily, since no one knew where they would land.
shots.B07C200S52H01: Footnote 252 notes that this verse is omitted in the Bombay text but is believed genuine.
shots.B07C200S52H02: Footnote 253 explains that celestial weapons act as living agents that abandon anyone whose death is near, even if invoked with the usual formulas.
shots.B07C200S52H03: Footnote 254 says the translator adopts the Bombay reading.
shots.B07C200S52H04: Footnote 255 explains that defeated men lose both worlds, this one and the next, by fleeing and committing sin.
shots.B07C200S52H05: Footnote 256 explains that celestial weapons were invoked by mantras to create the weapons desired, and that the Brahma weapon took the form of broad-headed arrows.
shots.B07C200S53H01: Footnote 257 explains that 'dharmadhwajin' literally means one who bears the flag of virtue, and so means a hypocrite who preaches virtue and acts otherwise.
shots.B07C200S53H02: Footnote 258 suggests the correct reading is 'aputrinas', not 'putrinas', and notes that the author of the Venisamhara play put this verse in Aswatthaman's mouth.
shots.B07C200S53H03: Footnote 259 notes that the last line of verse 37 differs in the Bombay edition, and Nilakantha accepts that reading as a license, though the Bengal reading fits better.
shots.B07C200S53H04: Footnote 260 gives the literal sense: the animals kept the Pandavas to their right.
shots.B07C200S53H05: Footnote 261 explains that Rama slew Bali during Bali's fight with Sugriva, though Bali had not wronged Rama, and that this act is regarded as a stain on Rama.
shots.B07C200S54H01: Footnote 262 says the original is expanded to make the sense clear.
shots.B07C200S54H02: Footnote 263 notes that a line of verse 23 is placed differently in the Bombay text and that Vishnu killed Hiranyakasipu without letting him speak, per the Vishnu Purana, and suggests a reading that fits Bhima's speech.
shots.B07C200S54H03: Footnote 264 explains that the Nishadas were, and still are, the lowest caste in India.
shots.B07C200S54H04: Footnote 265 says the Bengal reading is faulty and the Bombay reading 'this preceptor again' is adopted; Arjuna was Satyaki's teacher, so Drona was Satyaki's teacher's teacher.
shots.B07C200S54H05: Footnote 266 explains that kimpurushas were fabled creatures, half man and half horse, and that yakshas were superhuman beings living on inaccessible hills.
shots.B07C200S55H01: Footnote 267 says the translator adopts the Bombay reading of the second line of verse 35, which Nilakantha explains correctly.
shots.B07C200S55H02: Footnote 268 says the translator adopts the Bombay reading.
shots.B07C200S55H03: Footnote 269 explains, following Nilakantha, that the phrase means rising above the world and becoming detached from it.
shots.B07C200S55H04: Footnote 270 explains that the word means 'the terrible'.
shots.B07C200S55H05: Footnote 271 explains 'amritasya yonim' as the source of immortality, that is, of salvation, since the liberated become immortal with the Supreme Soul.
shots.B07C200S56H01: Footnote 272 explains that these are the five qualities perceived by the five senses, together with the natural elements in which they appear.
shots.B07C200S56H02: Footnote 273 notes that the weapon was given away to Rama, the disciple.
